Mr. Speaker, the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers and the Performing Right Society of England, with which are affiliated similar societies in eighteen European countries, organized the Canadian Performing Right Society, and to it assigned their alleged control by ownership and copyright of two million pieces of music.
Under the amended Copyright Act of 1931 this society is authorized to issue licences and to collect fees for the performance of any one of these two million pieces of music in a public place. subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF ENCOURAGING EMPLOYMENT OF WHITE SEAMEN IN PREFERENCE TO ORIENTALS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, February 26, consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Reid, to provide employment of greater numbers of white Canadian citizens on all

vessels of Canadian ownership and registry, the owners of which receive sums of money from the public treasury; and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Maclnnis.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF ENCOURAGING EMPLOYMENT OF WHITE SEAMEN IN PREFERENCE TO ORIENTALS
speechtext:
The motion submitted by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), with the amendment thereto proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), deserves perhaps a few words of comment, although, as the house knows, when the estimates of subsidies for the Atlantic and Pacific services were under consideration last week the question was discussed to some extent. For that reason I need not go into the matter very fully. I might, however, compliment the mover of the resolution and the hon. gentleman who proposed the amendment upon the zeal which they quite properly show with regard to the employment of Canadians on these vessels.
Perhaps I should refer to one or two misconceptions which I think crept into the debate. I think there was some thought in the minds of hon. members that, with regard to the Australian service, orientals were also employed on those ships. I am informed that only white men are employed on them; and in connection with this line, the Union Steamship line which we subsidize and of which the Canadian Pacific Railway is half owner, I am informed that recently twenty-four Japanese oilers and firemen were discharged and it was later discovered that these men were not only naturalized Canadians but were actually receiving union rates of pay.
After the debate the other evening and some of the objections raised in the house with respect to oriental labour, I got into communication with the manager of the steamship line and among other things received the following pertinent information- I will not go into it at any length to-day. He states that in order to replace oriental labour with white labour it would require the expenditure of nearly $800,000 additional; and as the proposed subsidy is only $600,000, it must be quite obvious that unless that subsidy were increased there would be no purpose whatsoever in the steamship company accepting any subsidy. The house would therefore have to decide whether, if it is the desire that all white labour should be employed, we should increase our subsidy to the extent of the added expenditure. To some that may not be very material; they may place above the necessities for economy the desirability of paying higher wages and employing white men.

Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Maclnnis
Further, I am informed that it would require about a quarter of a million dollars to make such alterations in these vessels as would be necessary for the accommodation of white people employed.	*
One other point made iby the management of the line was rather, I admit, a surprise to me. It is of very -considerable importance when the merits of the question are being discussed. It is that on the boats in the China and Japan services sixty per cent of the passengers are orientals. I was surprised to hear that the percentage was so large, and the significant fact that suggests itself is that if the personnel of the passenger list comprises orientals to the extent of sixty per cent-my hon. friends from British Columbia will admit this, I think-it would be somewhat difficult to get white men to serve these passengers.
I am not going further into the merits of the question, for this reason: in order that complete information may be obtained-and possibly some of these claims that have been made may be refuted-I move, in amendment to the amendment, the following, seconded by Mr. Elliott:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
"the question of the employment of Canadian citizens on ships and vessels the owners of which receive moneys from the public treasury of Canada be referred to the standing committee on industrial and international relations."

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, February 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Maclnnis to exclude from the country all persons belonging to those groups to whom we do not grant the full rights and privileges of citizenship.

subtopic: MOTION TO EXCLUDE FROM CANADA CERTAIN CLASSES OF IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
In closing the discussion on the resolution standing in my name, which was debated on Thursday last, I have not very much more to
say, except to take up certain points raised by some or possibly all of those who spoke against the resolution.
I shall first deal with the member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill). The hon. member was, I think, rather spiteful in his remarks on this resolution. He was not in his usual good humour. I do not think that his temper has been improved since he was taken over by the Liberal party. Very possibly his chagrin on this occasion was caused by the fact that, in the language of the street, he is on the spot, that the days of his whispering campaigns are over and that now he will have to face the issue squarely. He accused me of raising a dead issue, an issue which, he said, has been dead for thirty-three years. If that is so, why did he drag up the dead bones during the last election? Why did he rush from the city of Ottawa to his constituency of Comox-Al-bemi to advertise in an early address that the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation had stated that he was in favour of votes for orientals? Surely if the issue was dead he could have left it dead, without having to bring it up at that time and for his own special purposes.
He asks us, why not go to the source, that is to the provincial legislature? If the provincial legislature is the source, why was the issue raised in a federal election? I have here a copy of the Comox Argus of August 15,	1935. It gives a report
of a speech made by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi to a small audience on August 12. I find that on this occasion, he dragged in this dead issue, something that has been, to use his own words, "dead for thirty-three years." He is reported to have said:
Neither would he agree to advocate votes for orientals at the dictates of Woodsworth. When he first went to Ottawa he had worked hard to stem the stream of Chinese and Japs coming into British Columbia, and bad succeeded in stopping the Chinese entirely and reducing the Japs very greatly.
Unaided he did these things. This was the mighty Neill, speaking to his people in Comox-Albemi. Now notice this:
What would happen if they got the vote? They would vote solidly for the man or party who promised them more privileges and a larger quota of immigration.

I did not want to do it. We did not go out of our way to bring this up. They used the issue to serve their purpose, and now that it has served their purpose they want to bury it. Note that, sir,-the Liberal party is opposed to giving the orientals the vote. What a wonderful help such a statement will be in their negotiations with Japan to improve trade relations between the two countries.
I stated that in order to show the inconsistency of Liberal propaganda during the last election. I regret that the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) is not in his seat at the moment. One of the principal planks in his election campaign was that of better trade relations with the orient; and yet while he was using that as a plank in his platform, he was going through the country vilifying those orientals who are already in the Dominion of Canada. I was trying to show the inconsistency of it. However I am not going to take up any more time with the member for Comox-Alberni.
As to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), I wish to thank him for the way he approached this resolution when it was last before the house; and when he says that he was in no way connected with the advertising and the literature that I read in the house except that his photograph appeared along with the others, I accept what he said in the terms in which it was said. He states that he does not agree with the preamble. The preamble of the resolution is as follows:

Whereas it is detrimental to the best interests of Canada that there should be in the country groups to whom, because of race or religious beliefs, we do not extend all the right of citizenship;
That is quite clear, I think. It says it is detrimental, it is not in the best interests of this country, that we should have in the country groups of people whom, because of race or religion-and I would say, any other reason-we cannot admit into the full privileges of citizenship. H we are to have people come to this country, for what purpose are we going to have them here? Are we going to have them	come so that they	may	bemade citizens of this country, and to bring their children	up	as	citizens, or	are	weallowing them	in	for	some other	purpose?Are we going to try to bring in here a sort of inferior or slave class? I do not know. My friend from New Westminster says he is not in favour	of	the	preamble, but I	am
in favour of it: I am opposed to bringing people in here who will be in an inferior position to the rest of the community, because that inferior position makes them a constant menace to the people whom I represent. That is the reason I take that position.
The hon. gentleman stated that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation seemed to be losing a lot of sleep over the oriental franchise. Let me tell him that those who have lost the sleep must be those who spent their good money on campaign advertising in connection with this matter. We did not spend any money to advertise our position; we did not need to do it, the Liberal party did it for us. Let me say again that we have not raised this question in any shape or form, neither in the house nor outside the house. As a general principle we believe that every individual is entitled to certain rights and privileges in this country and from that position we cannot back down whether it brings us votes or whether it drives votes away. I am not so sure that my Liberal friends will be so keen on bringing up this question again at the next election, because during the past four years the people of British Columbia have been educated and the force of this movement has been largely spent.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated that he found it very difficult to understand my real objective. In order that he may have no doubt whatever as to what my real objective is I am going to read the resolution again in its entirety, and I may tell him that my real

Canadian Citizenship-Mr. Maclnnis
objective is exactly what is stated by the resolution:
Whereas it is detrimental to the best interests of Canada that there should be in the country groups to whom, because of race or religious beliefs, we do not extend all the right of citizenship;
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, the government should take the necessary measures to exclude from the country all persons belonging to those groups to whom we do not grant the full rights and privileges of citizenship.
I brought forward this resolution because I considered this matter extremely dangerous to the peace of the province of British Columbia, perhaps not so much now as later on, when we may have a larger population of those concerned in this matter, when they will be more vocal than they are at present and more ready to defend themselves. For that reason I do not wish to add to a problem that is already sufficiently serious by bringing into this country further immigrants from the countries concerned. Even if this resolution passes the house I do not expect that the government will immediately exclude any or all of those mentioned in the resolution by way of legislation. I assume that the Prime Minister, with his usual care in these matters, will take up the matter in the proper way and point out to the countries concerned the danger involved in allowing more of their nationals to come into this country before we have properly dealt with those already here. If it is done in that way I do not think we should have any great difficulty in dealing with the situation as far as it can be dealt with in that manner. I rather regretted the attitude taken by the Prime Minister the other evening in his statement as to the probable consequences of this resolution in the countries concerned. He said;
Like my hon. friend I deplore very much anything that is calculated to stir up racial feeling, but fortunately so far as political propaganda is concerned it is more or less localized. What my hon. friend forgets at the moment is that people in the orient who have never heard of our political discussions will read his resolution in the morning as a resolution that is being discussed in the House of Commons of Canada, and that makes it a very serious question indeed.

During the last session of the legislature at Victoria a resolution was placed on the order paper by a friend of the government, not a member of the party in power but a friend of the government, with the idea that it might embarrass the opposition. The resolution was to the effect that it was not in the best interests of the province of British Columbia that the franchise should be extended to orientals. That resolution was not allowed to be debated in the legislature; it was withdrawn, for the reason that they were afraid it might interfere with trade. Surely that is not statesmanship of a very high order.
Referring to the possible consequences of this resolution the Prime Minister also suggested that the happenings in this country were not of any very great import. Let me read what the right hon. gentleman said in 1924 when this question, in another form, was before this house. I quote from Hansard for 1924, volume 5 at page 4355:
I do not think one need argue the point as to the importance of encouraging Japanese students to come to our universities in order to become acquainted with our standards in matters of civic life; methods of government, and the like, and to return to the orient with those ideas. That, really, is the most effective kind of missionary effort-to let the oriental see the civilization we have, and if, in any particular, we are ahead, to let him carry those ideas back to his people.

How would the standards appear? Would they be anything after which the Japanese should pattern their civic affairs? I doubt it very much.

Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata) moved the second reading of Bill No. 6, to repeal the Economic Council of Canada Act, 1935.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my remarks on this bill will be very short. May I suggest to hon. members that they glance at the explanatory notes on the bill? There are two main reasons for this bill. First, neither this government nor the previous government have attempted to form an economic council. Secondly, there was an item of $20,000 in the estimates last year to cover the expenses under this act, but in the estimates for the coming fiscal year there is not a cent provided for that purpose. I therefore conclude that the government has thought it very 12739-37
wise not to take advantage of this legislation. The people of this country are strongly against it. Either the government or the cabinet is strong and good, or it is not. If the government is not so good, there must be a change. Well, Mr. Speaker, the change occurred on October 14 last, and now this legislation is completely useless. It is like a fifth wheel on a coach, turning idly, and it is just as well to dispense with it. I shall not deal with the matter further; I shall let the bill speak for itself. It is not a money bill; it is simply a lesson in economy. I hope the bill will meet with the approval of hon. members.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1-Repeal.

It seems strange that the introduction of a bill to repeal a measure concerning an important policy which was adopted only recently should be left to a private member on the government side. I think we should have some statement from the government in this connection. Last year I was in favour of the establishment of this economic council; I believed it was a move in the right direction. I do not know how the opposition feels towards this bill, but I want to register my protest against what to me seems to be a retrograde step.

Apparently the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) has never read the rules of the house. He is always fighting for freedom; he is always claiming he is persecuted by someone, but when a member submits a bill to the house on his own initiative he protests against it. Where is the logic in that action? It is the most absurd performance ever given by the hon. member. He is always fighting for his privileges. Last year when the then Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) objected to one of his bills he protested with tears in his eyes and thunder in his voice; he claimed he was being persecuted. I know the word "shameful" is not parliamentary, but if it were I would surely use it. I do not use it. I regret that the hon. member has outlived his usefulness in this house as a defender of the people's rights.

In response to the outburst to which we have just listened, may I say that I urged the other day that the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) should have the opportunity of bringing this bill before the house. I think he will recall that. I feel strongly as to the rights of any hon.

speechtext:
When the house adjourned on Monday evening I was about to reply to some of the observations which had been made by various members with reference to my motion. I was rather deploring the fact that a motion

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
dealing with a new economic set-up could not be introduced without a great deal of irrelevant talk. Again this year, as in some previous years, we have had the question of Russia dragged in. I fail to understand why a member in any section of the house cannot introduce a definite matter that seems to us to be of public concern without having someone rise and talk about Russia, as if this resolution in itself has anything to do with Russia. I am quite prepared to discuss Russia or Scandinavia or Japan on the proper occasion, but I do not think it is necessary to drag such questions into this discussion. I am glad to say that on this particular occasion none of us have been accused of atheism or free love or anything of that kind. I think we ought to learn in this house to discuss matters on their merits.
Again let me point out that a great many members have a very decided prejudice against the economic doctrine generally known as socialism. They have a right to their opinions, but the word socialism is not introduced in this resolution. Personally I have no quarrel with that word; it is a very convenient term that can often be set over against the individualism that now prevails. But the trouble is that there have been so many kinds of socialism in the past that the word lends itself to a great deal of confusion. We have had the socialism of Marx; there has been the socialism of some of the other European countries; we have had the socialism of Hitler, nazi socialism as it is called, the socialism of the bolsheviks and the socialism of the Scandinavian countries; and in England for many years we have seen the socialism of the British Labour party and other varieties such as fabianism and Christian socialism. So that when one uses a general term of that sort he is apt to lend himself to a certain measure of confusion. I have tried to avoid that and have not even mentioned the word.
We in the organization I represent have called ourselves the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. A cooperative commonwealth is our objective and we seek to attain it by orderly methods, and in this we distinguish ourselves very sharply from a great many of the types of socialism that have frequently been proclaimed. It seems to me therefore hardly fair for anyone to use the word, in relation to us, in a derogatory sense.
I have been long enough in this house to know that at least some hon. members do not wish to be unfair. I think it is hardly fair to attempt to rouse prejudices when we have not put up the proposition which hon. gentlemen are trying to knock down.

Other people say, "You are backing away from your position." Not at all; we have never advocated it. Now I come to the question asked me by my hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Wood). In outlining our policy-and I think he will agree that we have the right to determine our own policy-we have considered that the farmers were not exploiters but that they were among the worst exploited class, and that so long as they were carrying on individual farming operations and were content to do so, there was absolutely no reason why there should be any public ownership of farms. It is altogether different when we come to the banks, which we believe have exploited the people banks, which are great corporations tending to create a monopoly. Under these circumstances what we have advocated is that when institutions rise to a position of monopoly or near monopoly it is right that the state should take them over. That is our position. We say that when the very means by which we live are in the hands of other people it is high time for the state to

I should say with regard to the farmers' problems that we have advocated public control of marketing operations, and public ownership of abattoirs, stockyards, elevators and things of that kind because we believe that in this direction the farmer is exploited. If the time should come when in western Canada, for example, the mortgage companies take over large tracts of land and operate them as great company farms, it might very well be that we should then consider it was time for the state to intervene and take over farm lands.

speechtext: Is it not true that during the provincial election in Saskatchewan two years ago your party advocated the use lease system in Saskatchewan?

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
The question comes from Saskatchewan: is it true that two years ago the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in Saskatchewan advocated the use title system, I think was the term used. Yes; there was a meeting of the provincial council of Saskatchewan and they decided that the farmers in that province were so hopelessly insolvent that the best way to meet their difficulties was to permit any overburdened farmer voluntarily to come to the government and ask the government to take over his farm, reducing the value to something in line with what the farm was able to produce, giving the farmer a certain amount to cover his equity, and issuing interest free bonds to those who neld the mortgage. That was their plan at that time in Saskatchewan. No other provincial organization has adopted that plan. It was entirely a provincial matter, and perhaps the proposition is not an altogether unreasonable one. I remember being in Sas-

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
katchewan at the time and talking to a very well established farmer, who was not overburdened with debt, but he said that if the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation came into power in Saskatchewan he would be the first, as an independent owner of a farm, to make application to have his farm taken over in that way. The question was fundamentally whether the present Torrens title, permitting a man to become hopelessly mortgaged, was the best way of carrying on farms in Saskatchewan, or whether an alternative system could be set up under which one could voluntarily ask to be placed.
May I once again call attention to the terms of this resolution. Even my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) seemed to fail to grasp just what it stated. The resolution reads: that in the opinion of the house, industrial, commercial and financial organizations that are failing to function in the general interest should be taken over by the appropriate public authorities. I spent a good deal of time in quoting from the price spreads committee report to show that a great many of these institutions were, according to the evidence given before the committee, failing to function in the general interest, and it was because of that failure that I thought they should be taken over by public authority. That was a perfectly logical conclusion to which to come.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman give us the names of a number of these financial organizations or undertakings that are failing to function properly?

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
I suggest to the
hon. member that he read the price spreads report. I should like to commend the government upon their action with regard to the mills at Sherbrooke, and especially the Statement of their position which appeared in the press at the time. I think I am right in saying that the ground was taken that if some private concern failed to provide for the needs of the workmen employed and generally to function in the interests of the public, consideration might very well be given to the question whether it might be necessary for the government to take it over. I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce took very much the same position in his speech the other day, and I think the speech from the throne suggested that there might come a situation which would require state interference.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext: Take that particular instance: would the hon. member advocate that the government take over the mills at Sherbrooke.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext: And operate them?

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
Yes, decidedly.
They would have to. If they are failing to function in the public interest and if the company would not come to time, I should say, let the government take them over and either close them or operate them in the public interest. The government could very easily set up a commission.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
They might close
anyway.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
They might close. At any rate all that was necessary was a firm stand on the part of the government to bring that company to time.
In this country, as we all know, there is some little difficulty in carrying out any proposal of this kind because of the division of jurisdiction as between the dominion government and the provincial governments. I sought to safeguard that point by saying they should be taken over by the appropriate public authorities. I can understand that under our constitution some undertakings would have to be operated by the provinces; others by the municipalities. For instance, if we wanted to carry on the milling business or the distribution of gasoline it might very well be that this could be done by the provincial authorities. If we wanted to carry on bakeries, run street cars or anything of that kind obviously those matters could be best handled by the municipal authorities. On the other hand there are certain matters such as railroads, matters of general nation-wide public importance, that can be handled more readily by the dominion government.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I do not think this parliament is the body that would handle these different undertakings. Already in Canada we have gone a long way in the direction of administration by commissions. I think probably that is the line along which we had best advance, by commissions responsible to the government but which will not be interfered with in the day to day operations. I would add this, that I hope we may come to the point where our commissions will not be so largely political appointments and, further, when on the commissions there will be representatives of both the managers and the employees of the undertakings concerned. In a
582	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
general way, however, we will have to develop a whole series of administrative boards that will carry forward the detailed operations of socialized production and distribution.
I believe there are two ways in which operations along this line can be carried forward. The first is organization as a public service, as we now operate the Canadian National Railways, as the province of Ontario now operates the hydro electric system, and as the city of Toronto now operates its tramways. There are a great many institutions that lend themselves to that sort of operation, in fact they demand a very centralized control. But there is another class of undertaking that might very well be given over to cooperative enterprise. The other day one gentleman said to me that he could not quite see how the cooperative institutions, of which my hon. friend from Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) spoke the other day, fitted into our scheme. They fit into it precisely and naturally. We do not want to build up a great bureaucracy; there are a great many things that can be and should be done by cooperative enterprise. I am very happy indeed to point to those developments in Nova Scotia to which the hon. member for Grey-Bruce referred, by which some of the poor farmers, and especially the poor fishermen, whose plight was almost desperate a few years ago, are gradually making progress by taking over their own affairs and merchandising some of their own goods. That is an example of the producers' cooperative. We all have been heartily in sympathy with the idea of the pools in western Canada. I do not want to discuss the merits of the pools to-day; they have failed in some respects, but in my judgment their failure was due very largely to causes outside their control as also outside the control of the regular grain trade.
I should like to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that we believe in cooperative enterprises. We may have to start a good many of them and have some of them fail before we learn the best *way to carry them on. We are also heartily in sympathy with consumers' cooperatives along the line of the Rochdale system, which has been such a magnificent success in England and the Scandinavian countries; we think it might well be carried on here. The practical difficulty is that the big departmental and chain stores have got in, as it were, on the ground floor, and have developed to such an extent that it is very difficult for a consumers' cooperative to get on its feet. But we of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believe in these consumers' organizations. They constitute an integral part of our particular class of socialism.

A question that is often brought up-I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) referred to it the other day-is this question of liberty. I have a good deal of sympathy with the Liberal idea of personal liberty; I think I was brought up more or less to regard that as one of the most cherished possession of the British people, but I do say that under the circumstances now existing personal liberty is being gradually whittled down until there is not a great deal of it left. I want to quote once more the figure I mentioned the other evening, that outside of the agricultural workers five-sixths of the workers in Canada are working for wages; that is, as the saying is they are not "on their own." They are simply hired men, as it were, fortunate indeed if they can get a job but having very little indeed to say with regard to their wages, hours or the conditions under which they work; having nothing to say with regard to how the product produced under collective arrangements shall be sold, and having no claim on the profits that may be made. Under these circumstances we cannot talk very much of a man's liberty. It is true that he can still go to vote, though there seems to be a tendency towards depriving those who are not working of the voting privilege. But supposing a man can vote; that is a very small area of liberty. If somebody else owns the very means by which I live I am not a free man. The manager of a big concern, as the price spreads committee pointed out, is in the position of a mass buyer. He negotiates with and buys labour with somewhat of the advantage of a mass buyer, which is relatively a fortunate position for him but a very unfortunate position for the individual workingman.
To a limited extent trade unions have asserted their right to collective bargaining. On the railroads that right is recognized as it is in a few factories, but generally speaking it is not recognized across this country. Failing that we find the individual workman in a very bad position indeed. As I stated on Monday, under existing circumstances the labour man and the farmer or primary producer are exploited, the small business man is being crowded to the wall and the consumer-and we are all consumers-is being cheated, and has no effective protection. It seems to me clearly demonstrated that a great many of our big institutions are not working in the public interest.
We are told again and again that the choice is between individual enterprise on the one hand and bureaucratic monopoly on the other.

Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
That is not a fair way of putting it. As I have said, five-sixths of the people are not carrying on under the principle of individual enterprise; only one-sixth of the workers are doing that. That is one aspect of the case. On the other hand we are not advocating a bureaucratic monopoly. We want to release the energies of the people; we want to restore them to freedom, if indeed they ever had it. We want to see that they get freedom not merely in the sphere of politics but also in economic sphere, which is an altogether different matter. Without going into the political question to any extent I feel very strongly that the old Liberal party made a big step forward when it insisted on liberty in the political sphere, but I believe if they do not now go forward to advocate this other kind of liberty their party will become a thing of the past, just as the old laissez-faire economic doctrine on which Liberalism was built is already gone at least as a workable policy. Even the Minister of Trade and Commerce admits that state interference has become more or less necessary.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
Take for instance the
iron and steel industry, which represents approximately $100,000,000 or less in this country and employs many thousands of men; how would the hon. member operate it if taken over, if not under a bureaucracy?

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
I said a few
minutes ago it might be operated by a commission. To-day it is under the control of a private group; it is not operated by the
employees but by a little bureaucracy, a bureaucracy that is absolutely irresponsible.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
To-day it is operated
under the law of supply and demand.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext: No, I suggest that my hon. friend read the report of the price spreads commission, which clearly states that the law of supply and demand does not operate freely to-day. I do not say that supply and demand is not a factor, but monopolies, trusts, combines and international cartels have been built up; we have tariffs and quotas, exchange difficulties and all the rest, so that the old law of supply and demand under free competition has ceased to be a controlling instrument.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext: I am anxious to get the background of the hon. gentleman's opinion. If the government took over the iron and steel industry and it were operated under a bureaucracy, how would he protect that great industry from being overstaffed, most as we all know every government department is overstaffed? Then the iron and steel industry could not compete with the world, if it were overstaffed as a bureaucracy operated by the government.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
I have said I do
not want bureaucracy; I want free operation under something in the nature of a commission. There is a great deal of patronage in our big business institutions, just as there is altogether too much patronage in the government service. I am one of those who have pleaded that, we get away from patronage in the government service, but personally I do not think there is any more favoritism in the management for example of the Winnipeg municipal hydro electric than there is in the Winnipeg Electric, a private concern. I doubt if there is any more favoritism on the Canadian National Railways than there is on the Canadian Pacific. During the war, when we felt it was a life and death struggle, we took over a number of industries. Organizations and agencies were taken over on a very large scale in Great Britain; if they could be managed economically and efficiently during the war there is no particular reason why they could not be so managed under our democratic system, if only we have a little higher ideal of public service. To-day we have monopoly on every hand. I think it is conceded that the old condition, individual shopkeepers and producers and bankers, is largely a thing of the past. We have monopoly or a state of things verging on monopoly in nearly all our industries and in our financial concerns, and in a great many lines of commerce. There is competition in certain respects, but the competitors get together very readily under agreements in various forms. So it is not a question of individual enterprise versus monopoly. The question is whether this inevitable monopoly will be irresponsible, as it is to-day, and inefficient, as I claim it is to-day, and as I think the evidence before the price spreads commission amply bears out. Or will this monopoly be fascist in type? There is danger of that. As time goes on and these institutions get into trouble they come to the government asking for protection, for loans, for special privileges; they are apt to come and say: It is a matter of great public concern that we should continue to prosper. The result is that big business is closely tied up with the government. We do not want fascism in this country, I do not think there is one hon. member who would deliberately say he wants fascism here on the lines they have it in Germany, but if we tie up business and government we are making an approach to that sort of thing.
584	COMMONS
Cooperative Commonwealth-Mr. Woodsworth
There was great danger of that in connection with the new deal in the United States, and that is why some of us had to give only qualified support to the proposals of the late government; we thought their measures were moves in the right direction, but on the other hand we felt that there were certain dangers which had to be carefully guarded against. I have said that the practical alternatives before us are: Is this inevitable monopoly to be (a) irresponsible and inefficient, or (b) fascist in type, or (c) democratic? We of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation urge that it should be democratic in type, under the control of government, federal, provincial or municipal, or under the control of cooperative institutions, which are perhaps the very highest examples of democracy in industry. I need not say anything more at present about that cooperative ideal. I think it is right, it is desirable, because the consumer himself determines what he wants. I should like to see it encouraged. In Ontario last year the Liberal government passed legislation which made it fairly difficult for consumers' cooperatives to carry on. In practice those of us who have been keenly interested in free consumers' cooperative organizations have found that the forces of capitalism are so strong that they tend to crush such organizations. Furthermore the whole motive in business today is that of profit. Our belief is that the motive of profit must give way to the ideal of service, that the ideal behind business ought not to be primarily to make profit, as is now the case, and increasingly profit for a small group, but primarily to give service.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext: You want the millennium.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
Someone behind
sneers, "Oh, you want the millennium." Well, I want something better than we have to-day. I am talking in a very practical way-

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext: You are not talking business.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
No, thank heaven; I am not talking business. Someone sneers, "You are not talking business." I get disgusted with two classes of people in this house, one of which is composed of a large number who because they have legal training are always throwing it at the rest of us who are not lawyers that we cannot understand things because we have not had that great advantage of legal training. I am willing to concede the advantage of knowledge of the law, but I do not think the lawyers in the house have a monopoly of brains. The other thing

that annoys me is that certain people who have engaged in business, and have spent most of their time and energies in carrying on their own business, along their own lines-

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext: And giving men employment.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext: -when anyone suggests any change whatever, immediately say: Oh well, you don't know anything about business.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext: Neither you do.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
That may be, from my hon. friend's standpoint. But I am putting forward a reasonable proposition, a type of organization actually in operation to some extent in many parts of the world. The stupidest kind of people are those who always look to the past and think we cannot do anything better than follow the old lines. I am not one who wants to jump at every new thing that may be advanced, but I point out that one of the great laws of life is that we must change to meet new conditions, or die. Change or die is not only one of the great laws of nature, but of business as well. Even my hon. friend from Davenport to succeed in business doubtless found he had to modify his methods from time to time. I submit that the whole basis of business in this country will have to be materially modified if we are to succeed as a nation. I think in this house at least we ought to get away from the petty shopkeeping and small workshop idea and look at things from the larger national viewpoint. Only in this way can we adequately discuss general policies. Undoubtedly a great many of these gentlemen who criticize know a great deal more about the details of business than I do, but I rather resent being told so frequently that those of us who have spent the greater part of our lives studying social and economic questions are not in a position to advance a proposal that on the face of it at least seems reasonable.
There is just one other consideration I should like to advance-I wish I could have had a chance to develop it further in the time at my disposal-and that is with reference to the international situation. I am urging this resolution not merely for the welfare of Canada. I am profoundly convinced that it is only as we get away from the competitive principle in our international affairs that we are going to gain permanent peace. In the days after this capitalist system had been set up, we found that a few people were able to accumulate a very considerable stock of goods in excess of that which they could dispose of under the circumstances in their immediate

Small Property Holders-Mr. Deslauriers
locality, and so, quite naturally, other markets were looked for. I am not blaming any individual for that; I am simply tracing the natural development of affairs. Then as production grew, a greater expansion of markets was necessary to dispose of it, and so we developed our foreign trade. At that time I have no doubt that the policy of expanding trade-free trade, in a word-was fundamentally right from the standpoint of business. The Liberals in England came into a position of great prominence at that time, and if I had been living then I would have voted Liberal, as some of my people did, because conditions then were ripe for freer trade. The development went on and on until a good many other nations got into the same position, of seeking foreign markets, and once that point was reached, friction was constantly arising. In the last fifty years there has been friction on a good many occasions between European nations as each sought new markets in countries less developed. The continent of Africa was gradually carved up amongst the nations of Europe until to-day it resembles a patchwork quilt.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST
speechtext:
I am sorry to have to
interrupt the hon. member, but his time is up.

subtopic: CONCENTRATION OF ECONOMIC POWER-PROPOSED PUBLIC OR COOPERATIVE OPERATION OF UNDERTAKINGS FAILING TO FUNCTION IN THE GENERAL INTEREST

I must thank you,
Mr. Speaker, for reminding me. At some future time I should like to develop further this external side of the matter. I will close by reasserting our position. I do not believe that we can have permanent peace in the world until we arrive at some other method of doing business than by international competition, which, after all, is simply an extension of the competitive principle on which for a good many years we have been operating within our own country.

subtopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF THEIR FINANCIAL SITUATION LOOKING TO EQUITABLE TREATMENT
PROPOSED STUDY OF THEIR FINANCIAL SITUATION LOOKING TO EQUITABLE TREATMENT
speechtext:
[DOT]
Whereas small property holders in the cities are in a most critical financial situation;
And whereas during the past five years the depression has borne more heavily on this
class of citizens than on any other by reason of the unemployed who are dependent on public bodies;	.
And whereas they contribute substantial sums to the public treasury in the form of taxation;
And whereas the agricultural class is now benefiting by government measures;	_ .
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this bouse, the problem of these small property holders should be the subject of study in order to determine whether it is not opportune and equitable that they should receive the full consideration to which they are entitled.
Mr. Speaker, the problem dealth with in this resolution is not a new one, although it has acquired with time a far greater degree of acutence. I deemed it proper last year to insert in the Order paper of the house a similar resolution to the one now under consideration, with the intention of placing before the government of the day the sad financial plight of small property holders in villages, cities and, more particularly, in Montreal, and with the object also of making practical and useful suggestions to meet the difficulties created by the crisis. The correspondence which reached me at the time, together with that which I am now receiving, with reference to this resolution, have impressed me with the fact that the evil is greater and more general than I first thought.
Last year, a delegation composed of government followers, judging that the question involved was an important one, travelled from Montreal to Ottawa in order to interview the hon. Mr. Duranleau, then Minister of Marine. The latter replied to the delegation that he highly appreciated the step they had taken and that it was quite possible, even most probable, that before the end of the session the government would introduce a bill in order to come to the rescue of small property holders, the only class in the community which the government had forgotten.
This was as early as February 14; just after the Prime Minister had stated that the elections would come as a thief in the night and that government measures should be proceeded with as quickly as possible. The opposition, knowing the people's strong desire to be consulted at the polls with the shortest delay possible, did not object too strongly to the government's proposal to discontinue at this stage of the session, the study of private legislation so as to give precedence to government measures.
What happened? Well, we found out later. The government totally and deliberately disregarded the plea of small property holders and left them to their plight. However, members who sat in the last house will recall that instead of quickly despatching state affairs, senators and members were sent home
586	COMMONS
Small Property Holders-Mr. Deslauriers
for five weeks, that the house did not sit one single Wednesday evening during last session, that every holiday was observed, that the house adjourned in the middle of the week to allow the people's representatives to attend a cinema performance! And while the government was conducting the affairs of this country at a cost of S7.000 per half-day, celebrating and taking holidays, a large proportion of the population was on relief, famished treckers were wearing out their soles tramping from ocean to ocean, small property holders, having known but sacrifices without any compensation whatsoever from the government, were being, one after the other, despoiled of their property.
In 1932, for motives which I am not called upon to discuss at present, small property holders in the province of Quebec were deprived of all compensation in connection with the rents due by the unemployed, while in all other parts of the country it was just the reverse. Twelve months were required to ascertain whether the term "shelter" contained in the act included lodging for the unemployed; in short, it meant heavy losses for these small property holders who were compelled to meet their fixed charges. Though their rights were recognized later on, no payment was made of the amounts due to them for services rendered in 1932 to the publicly-assisted unemployed.
Most of these property holders had acquired their houses with savings that represented a lifetime of toil and self-sacrifice during a period when the cost of labour and of materials set the prices. The purchasing price at that time represented the true value of the properties; they could not have been acquired for less. They had not been paid double their value as in the case of farmers who during the war bought at inflated prices, land that has since dropped to its normal value. It was not lack of foresight on their part. That is an important point.
In the case of farmers, the crisis exerts its effects which are reflected in a decrease of prices on farm products, as compared with war-time prices and that is all.
In the case of small property owners, however, it is otherwise: they did not buy at inflated prices, and, ever since the height of depression, their property has from a revenue viewpoint, lost fifty per cent of its true value.
They have provided a shelter-and continue to do so-for poor unemployed people who are dependent on the state. Notwithstanding the fifty per cent decrease in value of their property, the municipal valuation has not been reduced; taxes of all kinds pile up on them. Municipal taxes have gone up; water,
fM. Deslauriers. 1
business and snow-removal taxes have doubled; and there are in addition special taxes, super-taxes, dominion and municipal sales taxes, etc.
Many of them have lost their positions and find themselves in the ridiculous situation of having to seek relief-which is denied them because they are property holders-while being compelled to give charity to people dependent on governments.
Every week, these small property holders are, one after another, despoiled by loan companies. If I am rightly informed, one company alone, known as the "Industrial" has, for its share, despoiled 3,000 of them. I know for a fact that rackets exist in Montreal accumulating wealth by preying on these small property holders, they were established by New York and Chicago racketeers. I could right now name one or two of these organizations; I shall give in a few minutes the result of their operations in a case which was brought to my attention. For instance, there is the Continental Guaranty Corporation and the Industrial Loan Investment, companies that advertise by means of the radio. I think, sir, it would be most appropriate for the government to appoint a commission of inquiry to look into their operations.
The government has in the past come to the assistance of the farmers.
I find no fault in this connection, I might even state that this class of the community has perhaps not received all the solicitude and consideration due to it. If, on the one hand we must admit that farmers deserve consideration, on the other hand, the class of citizens known as small property holders in cities are just as deserving of the government's sympathy. We should not remain unrelentingly indifferent towards the latter, but rather, recognizing the fact that they are taxpayers like all other citizens of Canada we should render them all possible assistance and prevent loan companies, such as those I have just mentioned, from exploiting them.
The Liberal party's policy will contribute, no doubt, to restore equality between all classes, providing the provinces and the dominion cooperate and providing certain provincial and federal laws are amended or repealed. For instance, drastic conditions in contracts, such as defesance clauses, should be prohibited; the term "responsible by mortgage" should be sufficient, if more study and consideration were given to transactions.
Australia, Belgium and the United States have passed excellent laws in connection with their small property holders. A glance at

Small Property Holders-Mr. Deslauriers
their legislation might perhaps help the government to legislate in the same sense.
I believe that measures could be enacted, especially in times of crises, so as to come to the rescue of small property holders certain terms included in contracts, such as "personally responsible" should disappear. In times such as these, when credit is lacking, city and country people have been victimized by this term "personally responsible," which has despoiled them of their furniture for the sake of a few hundred dollars which they borrowed and could not repay.
The government is in duty bound to study the possibility of long term loans at three or four per cent interest and of extending to small property holders in cities the privileges granted to the farming community. We have but to consult the history of France, at the period when the credit foncier was established in that country, to understand the eminently patriotic role that this group of French citizens played at a time when the peasant class was threatened with ruin. We could draw very profitable conclusions to the advantage of the small property holders and even of the farming classes, from the study of that page of history.
By mutual agreement with the provinces, it would be proper to establish a five year obligatory moratorium and, finally, to facilitate long term loans, at three per cent in order that these small property holders might borrow the necessary money to pay off arrears of interest and taxes.
I stated a moment ago that I believed that the co-operation of the provinces was absolutely necessary. I am quite certain that the hon. Minister of Labour and Public Works of my province could amend the labour legislation of Quebec and liberalize it in such a way as to provide employment for the man who, because he has reached forty-five years of age or more, finds it impossible to obtain work, and to legalize the stipulations of the contract in order that these workers may have a chance to earn a livelihood and not be looked upon as prematurely old at forty-five.
I stated, sir, a few moments ago, that rackets existed in the city of Montreal to the detriment of these poor workers who have spent all their hard-earned savings. I have before me correspondence referring to the Continental Guaranty Corporation. I shall read it, as I have been given permission to submit it to the house and make use of it as I thought fit:

Enclosed you will find a few documents relating to our conversation of Sunday last. You may, without fear, make use of them as evidenced in support of your resolution.

subtopic: PROPOSED STUDY OF THEIR FINANCIAL SITUATION LOOKING TO EQUITABLE TREATMENT
speechtext:
Mr Speaker, I want to compliment the hon. gentleman (Mr. Deslauriers), who represents one of the industrial ridings in Montreal, upon having the courage to bring this industrial question to the attention of the house at this time. As I too, represent an industrial riding, I feel I should say a few words in connection with this resolution. On three occasions last session I directed the attention of the house to the untold suffering and misery of the industrial worker of this country. He is suffering such privations as I have never seen before. Industrial workers in part of my own riding, in that of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) and in other parts of Toronto are suffering because of economic conditions over which they have no controh The industrial worker is just becoming a proletarian and the time has come when protection should be given to him all along the line and to all the people of Canada and not only to some. During the campaign I remember seeing throughout Ontario liberal billboards announcing that if the-people voted for so-and-so unemployment would be ended; that if they voted for so-and-so work would be pro-

vided for the worker. Attempts have been made by the creation of commissions to end unemployment, but the poor industrial worker still suffers.
Forty-seven per cent of the Canadian people are engaged in industry. Six or seven years ago parliament, not satisfied with incorporating bona fide loan companies and banks, permitted the incorporation of a number of shark loan companies. These companies are flourishing in almost every riding in the city of Toronto. As the former member for Battle River, Mr. Spencer, told the house last year, these shark loan companies are charging as much in some cases as thirty-five and forty per cent on second mortgages. Quite rightly parliament has given some assistance to the farmers in the prairie and other provinces, and to fishermen under the farm loan board, but similar assistance should be given to the industrial workers. The western farmer ate the sour grapes of free trade for twenty-five or thirty years while the grain exchanges, the middleman, transportation and elevator companies were robbing him of a fair price for his crop. Then the depression came along and he found himself suffering untold privation. I am sorry for him; I helped plead his cause, but I must also plead the cause of the industrial worker, as I said three times in the house in 1935, and asked for equality of treatment for the industrial worker also.
In the days of Laurier and Macdonald practically every man was a property owner. A man might own only a small store, a little mill or a shack, a cow or something else, but he was a property owner. He had a little garden on the back of his lot and while he might be working only three or four days in the week, he was as much a property owner as was the man who had large holdings. He was a citizen of the country and he had his property rights. Now it is gone. Those rights have been taken away, and one of the principal duties facing parliament at the present time is to pass some measure that will help in some way to solve the problem of unemployment and distributivism in Canada.
The government has so far brought forward no definite plan looking to that end; neither in the speech from the throne nor in any proposal that has so far been suggested do we find anything in that direction. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) read a speech yesterday in regard to the relief camps, which was out of order; according to the rules of the house he should not have made the speech he did except on the orders of the day. But the rules apparently are for some

Small Property Holders-Mr. Church
and not for others and they are badly in need of overhauling. At any rate, so far the government has brought down no definite plan to solve unemployment.
At the opening of parliament I handed a question to the clerk of the house but it never appeared on the order paper. I wanted to know what plans the government had this spring for providing useful employment for the great body of the unemployed, but that question, as I say, never found its way to the order paper. This was not through any fault of the clerk's, for he is a most able, capable and zealous and painstaking and popular officer. But why was not that question placed on the order paper? I know of no rule of the house that prevents a member of parliament from placing a proper question on the order paper. What does the government think private members are here for? Are we to sit here and listen to ministers introducing academic measures for dealing with the unemployment problem, leaving industrial workers in the meanwhile to starve or to go to the poorhouse or to be placed on relief?
In the district represented partly by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) and Greenwood (Mr. Massey) and also embracing the part of Toronto represented by myself, there are 300 industries, large and small, in which Canadian workers, and their fathers and grandfathers before them, have been employed and some have lived during all that time on the same property. Sixty-five per cent of the people in that area at one time owned their own homes, but hon. members would be surprised to know how many of them have lost everything. Mortgage companies can afford to put up skyscrapers, but when they come to deal with the industrial worker who is in straitened circumstances there is no hesitancy about sending him a lawyer's letter and foreclosing; and if he tries to get some assistance from one of the shark loan companies incorporated by parliament he finds himself faced with a demand for interest rates of 25 , 30 and 40 per cent. If he is unable to meet his liabilities he loses everything-his piano, bed, chairs and every other article of furniture, all under chattel mortgage at 10, 12, 15 and 20 per cent.
What is going to become of the industrial worker? Where is he going to end up? Unless the two old parties open their minds to new ideas and their ranks to men with new ideas, then I say that by 1940 or 1945 we shall have a socialist government in this country. I say that advisedly; I said it in the last parliament and I say it again. The
two old parties in the house must wake up to the realities of the present day problems just as the parties in England have done. Consider what the National government accomplished over there. They provided a measure of protection for the working population and built homes for them, balanced their budget and adopted a tariff that brought jobs and a housing policy.
With regard to the principle of the resolution, parliament has established a system of protection for the farmers under the farm loan act. If a farmer gets into difficulties there is a farm loan board to which he can turn and have some arrangement made with his creditors along new and more satisfactory lines. An effort is made to obviate foreclosure. That is quite proper; it affords a long overdue measure of protection for the farmer.
At the last session the plight of the fishermen was under consideration. Our fisheries constitute one of the greatest industries in Canada, but the fishermen have had a very hard time of it. The Bennett government of that day, 1935, introduced legislation for the relief of the fishermen, and when the bill was before the house I took occasion to plead the cause of the industrial worker. I supported the bill, because there was a farm loan board to which the farmers could appeal and I thought it only fair that the fishermen and industrial workers should also be given some consideration. I should like to read some of the remarks I made at that time:
The time is not far distant in this country when we shall have to set up for the industrial workers a board similar to those set up under this fishermen's loan act and the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act so that the retail storekeeper, the individual worker, and those engaged in industries will have some means of protection. A retail grocer who fails and whose little shop is gone or an industrial worker who gets out of work or is only on part time should be dealt with in the same manner as the poor fisherman or farmer; he should he able to secure similar protection. There ds no reason why forty-six per cent of the people who are engaged in industry should not have the same form of protection as is given under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, the fishermen's loan act and so on. There should be created for these people a similar board to establish long term mortgage credits even up to twenty-five years for the small retail grocer or the small industrial worker who is out of work or may be on part time as many of them are. Sooner or later we shall have to extend this very wise and commendable feature of this legislation. I would like to see some kind of board set up for the industries to which I have referred and some credit established either through banks, insurance companies, loan companies, mortgage companies or through parliament or partly through one and partly the other, for
590	COMMONS
Small Property Holders-Mr. Church
the protection and relief of the small industrial worker and the small storekeeper on the same basis as these other acts I have mentioned. We should have protection not only for the fishermen and for the farmers but for everyone; we want a system of protection that will take care of all the people. Those small industrial people who have lost their all by foreclosure or unemployment or high taxes are in the same plight as are the fishermen and the farmers, and the principle of this bill should be extended to them.
Speaking for an industrial province, I say that the industrial workers of this country are no longer going to stand for handling out protection to some and not to others. Under the provisions of this bill we are paying through the new fisheries board, taxes, mortgages, lien notes, security to the bank, hypothecation of the plant and equipment of the fishermen. The same principle of protection should be extended either through parliament or the banks or a board similar to the farm loan board to the industrial workers so that they will have a fair show under protection as we have it to-day to hold and retain their properties and their equities and their small business ventures.
The hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Deslauriers) is a physician and on that account he knows, better than most members do, what the industrial worker's condition is; no one knows more than the physician does what the worker suffers. I suggest, therefore, that he might urge upon the government the consideration of what has been done in England and the United States in the interests of the working classes. Steps have been taken in those countries to save the workers from foreclosure. Along the lake shore in the riding of York West there will be no vacant houses on the first of May. I plead with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), because I think something should be done in regard to this matter. No one wants to pay additional taxes, but it would not cost very much to bring in a measure of relief for our industrial workers, as the government can borrow at a low rate of interest to prevent foreclosures on industrial workers, the same as for farmers and fishermen.
