May I have a few minutes to speak to this motion and humbly make a suggestion to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers)? I think we are all very anxious to settle the problem of unemployment, and I take the liberty of telling hon. members who sit at the other end of the chamber that our anxiety to solve the problem is limited only by financial incapacity. I have heard from persons who, I must say, are sincere, many queer expressions of opinion such as these: We must act at once; we must meet the needs of millions; we must get them off relief; we must diagnose the trouble; then we must find the remedy, and then we must apply it. We should have some practical suggestions to make if we are going to take up the time of the house, and if we have some practical suggestions we should make them to our Minister of Labour.
To solve the problem of unemployment the only remedy at the present time, in my opinion, is more taxes and more expenditures, and I repeat that our financial capacity is limited. I think the business of the government is or should be conducted like the private business of any person. When we want to buy a horse or a house or a farm, the first thing we do is to look in our pocket or find out at the bank if we have the money to buy that horse or that farm or that house. If we have not the money we do not buy it; that is all, and the question of unemployment is on about the same footing. There are certain things that the government can
do and there are certain things that neither it nor the country can do. We ought to give the government time to make a survey and find out the difficulties and troubles in which we have been placed by the last administration in order that the government may bring forth the most practical remedy.
Allowing for an increase in our population, which fact accounts for an increase in the number of unemployed, I contend that the system which has been followed during the last five years has proved to be a failure. More people are working at the present time than were employed in the last few years, and yet there are more people on relief. Since 1930 we have spent, mostly on relief works, the enormous sum of approximately 8238,000.000. Perhaps those works were useful, and for that reason I am not going to say anything about them. But since 1930 we have spent another enormous sum amounting to S296.000,000 for direct relief pure and simple. Our country is large and rich and our population is rather small. Now, sir, if we must continue to feed and clothe and shelter so many people, and at such expense, naturally we shall have also logically to admit that our country is not so rich; that it has not such large resources and that it does not provide so many opportunities to our young people. But I make haste to state that I believe our country is both large and rich.
Older countries may not have the possibilities we have of settling their unemployed on the land and they may have to solve their problem solely by giving charity. But that is not the case with Canada. We have plenty of land, agricultural land, and I think it provides the way to solve partly at least our problem of unemployment. I believe even in prosperous years it would be sound political economy for the government to facilitate the development of our natural resources first instead of doing so much for the advancement of industries, the development of which is sometimes premature. There are many people in the cities who are waiting in vain for work which they cannot find in industries.
I have a plan or an idea which I submit to the Minister of Labour. We should make a survey of all the agricultural districts of our country-perhaps it has been made-and then we should divide those districts into lots or homesteads. Possibly I should preface the outline of my plan with certain remarks concerning colonization. People from the cities will not stay on farms which are covered with timber or brush; they will lose heart at the end of the first year when they see how little they have accomplished. The plan which I wish to submit to the house consists particu-

Unemployment-Mr. Brunette
larly of taking from the cities those people who have already had some experience on farms and putting them on the land. All the colonization plans that I have known of in the past were faulty because they gave the settler the impression that he could live for four or five years on that homestead or new land with subsidies or moneys that were to be given him by the government, instead of looking to the productivity of the land to supply him a living.
Having surveyed our agricultural districts and divided them into lots, we ought to take our unemployed or a portion of them from the cities and make them work to improve those lands, cut the brush or clear the land or possibly make some other improvements. I will not discuss the degree of improvement that should be made; if necessary we should conscript some unemployed for work on these farms and pay them decent wages. The settlers would then go on these farms which would almost the first year be productive. I can imagine the great development of our country we would have made in the last four or five years if only part of the money that has been spent for direct relief had been spent on the improvement of these raw lands. This would also have made it possible for people from the city, who have known better days, to go on those partly improved farms, come to like farm life and make their permanent residence there. I do not think I am mistaken when I say that Mussolini has opened up one or two provinces by following this system, and to-day those provinces are a source of wealth for Italy. We have given protection to industries ever since Sir John A. Macdonald inaugurated his national policy. Why not encourage a movement such as this? After all, farming is an industry. We have been protecting our industries because they were called infant industries. I believe some of them at the present time are elephants, and white elephants at that.
By following this suggestion I think three advantages would become evident. We would provide for some of our unemployed, for the time being, work for which they would be paid reasonable wages; we would promote the back-to-the-land movement and we would provide permanent places of abode for a great many people now unemployed. I believe more people on the farms would mean more taxes with which to pay our national debt. These people would buy a great variety of articles and in doing so would encourage, our industries. These same people, if they stay in the cities, will only cause us to spend

a great deal of money for relief; they will do nothing good for themselves, for their families or for their country.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I submit that our national wealth, confidence, courage and cooperation are the four levers that will help most gradually to solve our problems of unemployment. Our natural wealth, consisting partly of agricultural land, will provide work for a while and later permanent homes for many of our unemployed. The people of Canada have clearly manifested their confidence in the present administration. Our people have inherited that virtue of courage which was displayed so nobly by our ancestors on many occasions; courage in the mass of the people will respond to courage on the part of our leaders, and that cooperation which, I believe, was mentioned in the speech from the throne, if put into practice by all concerned-our party leaders, the heads of our provincial governments, the heads of our industries and the workers themselves-will soon put this country on the path of progress and happiness.

Mr. Speaker, I feel like occupying a very brief space of time in which to express a few words of commendation for the subject matter of the resolution, with one or two minor exceptions, and particularly for the manner in which the mover presented his case. I have rarely heard in the house a more moderate, more carefully reasoned speech, so full of material appropriate to the subject, and whatever may be our individual opinions about various matters, nothing but good can come from a presentation of a subject in the manner in which the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) presented his case, from a discussion on such a high plane and from a similar degree of intelligent study and earnest consideration of the questions involved.
I should like to say to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brunelle) who has just taken his seat that I think his observations might very well be added to the resolution as an additional suggestion for the solution of the problem. There was food for thought in his remarks. He did suggest, and quite properly, that we should consider the cost in this matter, and I gathered that his inference was that the mover of the resolution and others who might support it were a little reckless in their suggestions for expenditures without considering costs. I recall that a day or two ago another hon. gentleman made an excellent speech in which he directed particular attention to the fact that any expenditure that might be made in

Unemployment-Mr. Stevens
a certain way, similar to this, would have to come out of the pockets of the taxpayers. In that he was quite correct, but I would invite those who stress the danger of incurring costs to consider this: In the first place, are we now spending wisely? In making that query I am not casting reflections on the activities of the government for the past five or six years; I am speaking rather to this country as a whole, to this parliament, to the provincial legislatures, to the municipalities and to all those who are responsible for dealing with these great questions of unemployment and relief. I think we might well pause and ask ourselves if we have been spending wisely.
It may be that it could be argued that the emergency seemed to call for certain measures of prompt relief, and so forth, but now or at some other time we must stop to take stock and see whether we have spent wisely. The hon. member for Champlain, who has just taken his seat, suggested that we had spent some $238,000,000 on relief works and some $296,000,000 for direct relief. I am quoting his figures, which I have not verified but which I accept as correct, so in round figures we have spent about $530,000,000 for relief. If we could turn back five years and start out with the object of spending $500,000,000, could we act more wisely? I think most of us would say that we could, and I think we can say that without casting reflections on anyone. So it is not out of place to pause and invite consideration of some other method of dealing with the problem. Indeed I think the government is to be commended for the excellent statement made yesterday by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), and I hasten to take this opportunity to compliment him upon it. That is a wise move, a very wise move; I invite the Minister of Labour to consider further the principle he has therein enunciated and the possibility of applying it to some other lines of activity. I commend him and I commend the government for their action; I think it is a sane and practical step. But that does not alter the fact that this resolution also offers some wise suggestions, and I wish to spend a few moments in a brief analysis of it.
May I preface my observations with an invitation to the government to give earnest consideration to this resolution. It is not necessary to accept it in toto, but it contains some good suggestions and I think it deserves favourable and thoughtful and sympathetic consideration. In the first place I would suggest that when we invite the government to take full responsibility, a suggestion with which I fully agree, we ought 12739-39
to make certain exceptions. I suggest, for instance, that we should leave with the municipalities and the provinces the responsibility for normal charitable work. I am not speaking of unemployment as we generally understand it, and I suggest that we must define that term more carefully; I am speaking of the normal needs of people in all our communities. I suggest that we take the average, say for the five-year period from 1926 to 1930 inclusive and use that as measuring the cost of caring for the aged and sick and indigent persons that unfortunately we have with us at all times.
The next suggestion that should be made is that if the federal government assume full responsibility, which by the way they are largely doing now, either by guaranteeing loans or actual participation, then there should be some prohibition of the provinces enlarging their expenditure to fill up the gap made by the dominion government taking over the whole cost of relief. In other words there should be an understanding with the provinces that they are not just going to make a Roman holiday with the contributions that may be entailed by that suggestion. With those two provisions I would favour the federal government taking over unemployment relief. By that I mean the relief arising out of modern industrial and economic conditions; a narrower and more precise definition could be found. But some protection of that kind must be provided before the principle suggested in the resolution is accepted.
Then I commend very earnestly the excellent presentation made by the mover of the resolution in relation to mechanization. Perhaps I may be pardoned a personal reference; in the election of 1930 when unemployment was just commencing-it had been under way some nine months-I was asked this question in a public meeting: Did I believe that the party I was then associated with could provide for employment of all the unemployed? And I answered: No, I did not think they could, for some time at least. And the reason I made that answer at that time was that we had as a country given no serious study to the problem of displacement of men by machines. There was sporadic study by individual economists; some interested sociologists were giving dissertations about the matter, but no authorities had fastened their teeth into the problem of how to take care of those displaced in industry by mechanization, and we have not yet started such a study; nor have they in the United States. I am not able to speak with the same assurance in regard to all the European



Unemployment-Mr. Stevens
countries, but I doubt whether any country in the world has yet definitely fixed upon a solution cf that problem. The hon. member who moved the resolution very properly called attention to that, and I think we certainly should give earnest consideration to it, because, as he pointed out, the curve of displacement by mechanization is rising at an annually increasing ratio. I do not know where we shall arrive if we continue to drift as we have been doing in this and other countries in regard to providing for those so displaced.
There are those among my friends of the Social Credit group who argue that- the very essence of this vast problem is found in the credit structure and the financial and monetary system. There is a measure of truth in that. As I have intimated before, I am perhaps not prepared to go the full length with them, but do not let us brush these hon. members and their particular pet theories, if you like, aside in a sweeping manner as if there was nothing in them, as I have noticed a number of hon. members speaking in the house this session are rather inclined to do. I believe there is a germ of truth in what my hon. friends are bringing so forcibly to the attention of the country. I repeat, I do not go along with them fully in their theories and the mechanics of their system, but in the sphere of credit and monetary control is to be in part at least a solution of that phase of the question.
But in the resolution there are two very practical proposals which I desire to emphasize and support; that is in regard to housing and reforestation. It is twenty-two or twenty-three years ago that I first brought to the attention of the house the hopeless manner in which we are dealing with the great forest wealth of Canada. If time permitted I could tell hon. members how in British Columbia since I went there forty-two years ago I have watched the vast areas of primeval forest of the richest and most prolific kind being swept away and nothing but devastation and a wilderness left in its place. I have travelled across this continent some two or three hundred times,-I have lost track of the number-but coming from Fort William right to and beyond the city of Quebec one sees year after year these vast areas where the timber has been swept away, and what little soil there was is gradually being washed into the streams, and it will never be possible to reforest a great deal of that area. Again I would request hon. members to pause and ask themselves: What about fifty years from now in regard to the forest wealth of Canada?

Yes, but that does not alter my point at all. There is in British Columbia, too, a great deal of timber that is what they call ripe and that should be harvested, but there is a vast difference between harvesting timber in a sane and scientific way and slaughtering the wealth of the forests as we have been doing during the last forty years Despite what the interjection would imply, the fact remains that we are doing next to nothing in the way of reforestation. I am not going to enlarge upon that subject because it would take too long, but I want to say this, that there is a splendid opportunity for the investment-the investment, I repeat-of public moneys and the giving of work in a fine occupation which, as the mover of the resolution so aptly said, would be something that was self-liquidating, not next year or within five or ten years from now, but in thirty or forty or fifty years. There will be many a person in Canada in the years to come who will look back over this period of the last ten or fifteen or twenty years, and ask what on earth the people of this period were doing that they did not engage more earnestly in this great reforestation scheme. I invite the Minister of Labour and his colleagues earnestly to consider the suggestion of reforestation as one of the methods of solving this problem of unemployment intelligently.
The other matter to which I wish particularly to call attention is that of housing, and here again I shall be brief. If we launched now upon a national housing program, including slum clearance, the erection of workmen's houses, farm houses, and general housing such as already is involved in the act passed last session, I believe this would take us ten years and even then we would not have caught up with the normal decent requirements of the housing situation in Canada. I do not know why this is-I am not necessarily just referring to this house-but as Canadians we seem to fail to see the opportunity that rests in housing for providing a measure of relief in regard to this unemployment problem. Furthermore, there is no class of occupation in which money may be invested which results in more work for labour than building and housing; you can carry it right down to the production of the logs, cement, bricks and so forth. Everything you put into a building, everything you touch, every dollar that goes into it, ultimately will find its way to labour,

Unemployment-Mr. Poole
and so I say that there is a great possibility there, and I would strongly urge upon the government a real forward movement in housing. Let us not just play with the thing. The bill passed last session had its merits, but it does not touch the problem. We need a really earnest concentration of effort by parliament upon this problem of housing, which I believe, together with a few other activities such as the one mentioned by the minister yesterday, reforestation, the suggestion made in regard to settlement, and a few other movements of that kind, would rapidly absorb the unemployed of this country.
Would it be too trite a suggestion if I were to remind the house of this? There are only three major activities that underlie, shall I say, the interchange of human labour-the providing of food, the providing of clothing, and the providing of shelter. Anything beyond that is, if not a luxury, something more than an absolute necessity, but those three are absolutely necessary, and it is by an interchange of labour in providing those necessities that we lay the foundation of society. The business of parliament, of course, is to see that the balance is held fairly, and that is where the theories of the control of credit enter in and form such an important factor. Parliament must see that the balance is held fairly between those who control credit and wealth and those who need these things to which I have referred as absolute necessities, and I commend that phase of the question to my friends on the treasury benches.
The next suggestion in the resolution is for a living wage. No one will criticize that. I think we all realize that the providing of work at just enough for sustenance is not a solution of the problem because what is scarce to-day in this country is purchasing power. The agriculturist, through the low price he receives for his products, has not sufficient purchasing power to do more than barely keep body and soul together. He cannot purchase the implements, the clothing, the furniture that he would like to have and should have to-day. The very essence of democracy in my opinion is this, that the primary producer, particularly the farmer-and you can carry it on down to the fisherman, the lumberman and the miner- shall be paid for his effort sufficient for a decent livelihood. That I think is the very essence of democracy.
The second point is equally important, and that is that those workers who are engaged in the actual production or transportation or distribution of these things should be paid a wage which will enable them to live decently. Those two factors are essential if we are to have a healthy democracy. And, Mr. Speaker, 12739-39i
this resolution suggests that these employees should receive a living wage.
I am not going to go further into the question at this time, but I believe that if these matters are given earnest attention, and if the will to do them, the will to accomplish, is behind them, much may be accomplished. May I say with all kindness and all humility that we should drop perhaps the habit over the years we have formed in the house of looking backwards and forwards across the floor, and because someone here or someone over there makes a suggestion, of someone over there or someone here sneering at what is proposed, for it does seem to me, that we as adult and supposedly sane individuals act very often like a bunch of children when we are dealing with the well-being and the welfare and the bodies and souls, as one hon. member has put it, of human beings. Too often we treat these problems as if they were legitimate subjects to be bandied backwards and forwards on a partisan basis. I am accusing nobody, but I do say out of a long experience that we-and I include myself

are too prone to view these matters from that angle.
I suggest that the resolution in its principle and in its spirit, not in all its details, might be approved by the house and might form, shall I say, the basis for a coordinated effort on the part of parliament to do something towards a solution of this terrible problem of unemployment.

maintopic: PROPOSED PROGRAM OF PUBLIC WORKS AT TRADE UNION RATES OF PAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad of this opportunity to speak to this motion. It is important because again we have an opportunity of discussing one of the scars on our present system, and we find the suggestion made to-night that we apply a little more ointment. I was surprised to hear the suggestion made in the house to-night that we conscript the youth of this country and place them on the farm, and further that we should encourage people to go back to the land. There has been developing in the west over a period of years a situation which has caused much concern to the provincial governments in their efforts to help stay on the land people who have been farming there for twenty and thirty years.
This resolution suggests that we have a problem of unemployment. Unemployment is the reflex from a certain economic condition; in itself it is the cause of nothing. We hate been in the habit of saying that we cannot find employment for our people and we suggest or infer that there is some particular virtue in employment. What has happened during the past five years? The Dominion of Canada has spent approximately $592,000,000 in connection with unemployment
Unemployment-Mr. Poole

relief, and our problem is greater to-day than it ever was. Every time this question is raised in the house there comes up the predominant problem of money. Parliament is governed in its ability to do anything by its ability to extract taxation from the people. As time goes on this ability will become less; that is inevitable. We tried out a scheme of public works but found that it was costing too much for materials and was not meeting the requirements. Various suggestions have been made as to what can be done, but I say that this situation will continue while we continue to focus our attention upon unemployment as a problem. What is the economic system for? Is it to find employment? If it is, then this problem should have been solved long ago. An economic system should produce the maximum amount of goods and distribute them to all; its purpose should not be to find employment. Employment is incidental to production. The very fact that we have so much unemployment in this country and throughout the world proves that we are wealthy. We have accomplished that which man down through the ages has endeavoured to accomplish.
To anyone who dispassionately surveys the trend of events, it becomes more and more evident that government is nothing more than an administrative body to carry out the will of finance rather than the will of the people. We speak of democracy in one breath and then we speak of conscription in the next. What purpose is there in trying to keep afloat a ship that should have long since been sunk? Democracy is a splendid ideal for which Anglo-Saxons have fought down through the years, but I am convinced that more fighting must be done before we can enjoy a practical democracy which means, in its broadest terms, not just the freedom to vote, not just the right to walk the streets unmolested, not just the right to worship as we may or work as we will, but freedom from all restrictions that would otherwise impose the will of others upon us. Democracy is the freedom of the individual to pursue happiness and culture free from all influences detrimental to these objectives. To-day we are passing through a period strange to any age, strange because our environment is changing, not because people have desired these changes but because science has thrust them upon us.
Parliament is supposed to be composed of a body of men who have received instructions from the people of Canada to bring about certain results. The result demanded by the people at the last election was prosperity. It was not the business of the people to go into details as to how this prosperity should be brought about; it was the duty of the

government to make use of those experts who know just what to do. It was the duty of the government to introduce legislation to bring about this end. The people demanded that the government bring down legislation or have laws enacted, which, when given effect to, would make available to the Canadian people the wealth of Canada, whether it be produced by hand, brain or solar energy. However, this is not being done, not because all the people who have been sent here are insincere but because the individuals who go to make up a government persist in moving along orthodox lines. Any hon. member who may be more enlightened than the rest, who may feel the responsibilities placed upon him by the people he represents and who dares to give expression to his views may soon be reminded that he belongs to a party and must act in the interests of the party. In so doing he elevates partyism and submerges the principles for which he was elected. The people of Canada asked the government, in language that was unmistakable, to bring about prosperity, to remove any or all of those barriers that stood in the way.
I recognize the difficulty that any government faces to-day. I realize the necessity for a transitional policy. I say "transitional" because I know we are having thrust upon us new conditions to which we must adapt ourselves, but in the meantime the greater portion of our citizens are suffering privation and want in the midst of plenty and potential plenty. Many schemes have been tried out and many volumes have been written suggesting to the various governing bodies just what they should do. We have built up in six years a system of camps as a means of looking after one portion of our problem. These camps were tolerated only because we felt they were of a temporary nature. However, they have now taken on the nature of a permanency. Their purpose in the first place was to provide a cheap means of feeding those who had been displaced by better industrial processes, coupled with a declining market for export goods and the ever diminishing demand for labour. There are those who believe sincerely that our only hope lies in a greater export market. No doubt it would help for a time if those markets were obtainable, but I do not believe they are. I look at the world to-day and I see its tremendous ability to produce an abundance plus the policy of every nation of self sufficiency. Surely our experience has taught us that the methods by which we obtained markets in the days that are gone are no longer available. We must realize that our problem is internal; that the only value of an export market is the means

Unemployment-Mr. Poole
of exchanging our surpluses for the goods which are not common to the production of Canada. But this connot be done until we have monetary reform. Until we recognize that money in the final analysis is nothing but a ticket; until such time as we place in the hands of the people the tickets or tokens equal to our total price values, the complexities of this administration will be increased and the poverty of the Canadian people will become deeper and more widespread.
We have expressed so much concern for the economic rash. We are endeavouring to suppress it but we must know that there is no cure that way. You cannot feed your people when you must borrow to do so. By borrowing, you force the people of the future to carry a heavier load and mortgage the future. There is no cure that way. The disease goes much deeper than the skin; it is concerned with the vital processes of the body politic and to avoid substituting a more lingering horror it is necessary to restore these vital processes to health and balance functioning. The first act of the government should be to recognize the needs of the people and accede to their demands. First, they should find out what can be done, and then proceed to do it. Before this can be done we shall have to eliminate many traditional dogmas. I might add that the dogmas to which I refer do not belong particularly to the government benches.
Probably one of the greatest fallacies of the present generation is one most commonly expressed: I want work! This is repeated by governments when they say: We have an unemployment problem; we must put our people to work, the usual excuse being: We must give the taxpayers some return for the money they are spending. The people are thus led to believe that work has a particular virtue and that it will cure everything if we will just accept enough of it. The implication is that the sole purpose of an economic system is to find employment, while money is spoken of with reverence as though it had a quality superior to all things mortal or immortal. This is further emphasized as we review the attempts of governments to do something when the very thing without which we can do nothing is locked up in the tabernacle and the high priest demands that all who would use must first of all genuflect, and all must agree to be enslaved for all time. And if you protest you lose your respectability and are termed a radical, and you are referred to in a tone that suggests dishonour.
Is it the purpose of the government to find
employment? And having created it, do they believe that all will be well with the people? If this be true then it is high time we scrapped the machine and hanged on the highest tree every scientist living to-day, because he is detrimental; he is unemploying men at a rapid rate, He is responsible for this national or international calamity; he is responsible for all the misery and poverty in the land, because government policy is one which dovetails into that philosophy that belongs to the dark ages-Men must work to live. The golden age of the world was before the advent of the machine, those glorious days when men worked from the cradle to the grave and when dying gasped out, "Thank God I avoided starvation."
After all, it is not long since the ignorant of the jungle and of the plain burned and slew men who practised white magic; it is not long since we burned Joan of Arc at the stake as a witch because she showed a courage that was unusual; it is not long since the people thought the world was flat, and just a few short years ago a large group were insisting that those crazy Wright brothers be placed in some mental institution because they were trying to build some infernal contraption to fly. But did you ever hear of a people, or I should say a government, who told men that they could not eat their fill because there was too much? This sounds very much like that Irishman who said, "Don't come down that ladder because I have taken it away."

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
